opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so mode collapse is something I've become increasingly worried about, partly because it's so easy to overlook when you're just looking at benchmark numbers. The basic phenomenon is that after post-training, especially with RLHF and preference optimization, models tend to converge on a fairly narrow set of outputs. You ask for a story, a poem, a joke, or even an opinion, and you get something that's fluent and perfectly reasonable, but it's the same flavor of reasonable over and over again. If you sample a hundred times, you don't get a hundred meaningfully different answers. You get variations on a handful of templates.

Part of why this matters is creativity. Human writing is wonderfully diverse. Different people bring different perspectives, styles, and quirks. When models collapse onto the "average" or most preferred mode, you lose that long tail, and the long tail is often where the interesting, surprising, genuinely novel stuff lives.

But I think the bigger concern goes beyond creative writing. It's about pluralism. Human values and opinions are diverse, and there's often no single right answer. If a model has been aligned toward one narrow mode of response, it implicitly encodes a particular worldview, often reflecting the preferences of a relatively small group of annotators or a particular cultural default. As these systems get used by hundreds of millions of people, that homogenization can feed back into society. People read the outputs, write in that style, think in those framings, and that text becomes training data for the next generation of models. So you get this kind of feedback loop that can flatten human expression over time.

There's also a practical, technical side. If you want to use models to generate synthetic data, or explore a space of hypotheses, or do search and reasoning over many candidates, diversity is essential. If every sample looks the same, sampling more doesn't buy you much. So mode collapse undermines a lot of the techniques we rely on for scaling up reasoning and data generation.

And what's interesting is that the pretrained base models actually have a lot of this diversity. They've absorbed the richness of human text. So in some sense the alignment process is trading away something valuable in exchange for helpfulness and safety, and I don't think that trade-off has to be as steep as it currently is. That's why I think it's worth studying carefully, both to understand where the collapse comes from, whether it's the reward models, the preference data, or the optimization itself, and to find ways to recover diversity without giving up the benefits of alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended requests such as stories, poems, jokes, and opinions yield repeated variations on a handful of templates, despite the diversity of possible answers.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prompting a model to give a random number between zero and ten or describe that output as nonrandom.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. So, mode collapse is one of those things that sounds like a technical footnote, but I think it actually cuts to the heart of what we want from these systems.

Here's the basic picture. When you train a model with maximum likelihood and then decode with something like beam search or greedy decoding, you're pushing toward the most probable continuation. And the most probable continuation, averaged over the whole distribution of human text, tends to be bland, generic, repetitive. We saw this really clearly in the GPT-2 era, where beam search would produce these degenerate loops: the same phrase repeated over and over. That was part of the motivation behind nucleus sampling in our earlier work, the observation that human language is actually quite surprising, token by token, and if you only ever pick the top of the distribution you get something that no human would write.

But the concern has evolved. With RLHF and preference tuning, there's a different kind of collapse happening. You're optimizing against a reward model, and the reward model has a preferred style, a preferred register, a preferred set of safe answers. So the policy learns to concentrate its probability mass on a narrow slice of outputs. Ask a tuned model to write a poem a hundred times and you'll get essentially the same poem with minor variation. Ask it for a joke and you'll get the same handful of jokes. The diversity that existed in the pretrained distribution gets squeezed out.

Why does that worry me? A few reasons. One is epistemic. Human knowledge and human values are plural. There isn't one right answer to most interesting questions, and a system that always converges on a single modal response is implicitly erasing that plurality. It's presenting a consensus that doesn't actually exist. That's related to the work we've done on moral and social reasoning, where we found models tend to flatten disagreement into a kind of confident majority view.

Second is creativity and usefulness. If I'm using a model to brainstorm, to explore a space of possibilities, collapse is directly counterproductive. I want the long tail.

And third, more speculatively, there's a feedback loop concern. As more of the text on the internet is model-generated, and models are trained on it, you can get a compounding narrowing of the distribution. Each generation collapses a bit further. So I see mode collapse not just as a decoding problem but as a question about what kind of relationship these systems have with the diversity of human thought, and whether we're building something that reflects it or something that homogenizes it.

r001.rationale: The response says interesting questions often have no single right answer and tuned models concentrate on a narrow slice of outputs, reducing diversity.

r002.rationale: It discusses narrow, repetitive outputs generally, but does not state what happens when a model is prompted to give a random number from zero to ten.

astra-6.text:
The concern is that there are many valid ways to respond to a question, but the model can gravitate toward a narrow set of answers that are very likely or broadly preferred. Those answers may sound fluent and reasonable, so you don’t necessarily notice what’s missing.

But if we want these systems to help us explore ideas, we need more than the most conventional answer. We need different perspectives, different hypotheses, and sometimes an unusual idea that turns out to be useful. If generation keeps collapsing toward the same kinds of responses, we lose that diversity.

And this is particularly important when there isn’t one correct answer. A model’s tendency to produce a particular viewpoint shouldn’t be mistaken for consensus, or for the full range of ways people think.

r001.rationale: It says many valid responses exist, but the model can gravitate toward a narrow set of answers and lose diversity.

r002.rationale: It does not mention prompts to give a random number between zero and ten or say those outputs can be nonrandom.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that there are many different ways to give a good answer, but the model can become biased toward a very narrow set of answers. So the output may be fluent and look reasonable, yet we lose diversity in the ideas, perspectives, and reasoning that it can express.

And that matters because the most likely answer is not necessarily the correct answer, or the most creative one. For an open-ended problem, you want to explore different possibilities. If the model keeps returning to the same familiar patterns, we may mistake that consistency for intelligence, when it’s actually limiting what we can discover.

r001.rationale: It says many different answers can be good, yet the model may return a narrow set of patterns, limiting possibilities on open-ended problems.

r002.rationale: It does not mention prompting the model for a random number between zero and ten or describe its output as nonrandom.
